title: Long-tail surgical latency inspection — Cygnus Industries
topics: batch window sizing and latency budgets
VPC/on-prem network hops and cross-AZ egress

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-09-05 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samira Gomez (Redwood SE), Mark Rivera (Cygnus Head Infra), Lina Cho (Cygnus ML Lead), Jamie Torres (CTO), Omar Patel (SRE), Nina Berg (Product)

[00:00] Ethan: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick agenda, we want to walk the p95/p99 decomposition you saw in the dashboard, dig into streaming vs nonstreaming for your use case, and then go through KV hotkey concerns and network hops. um, any additions?

[00:18] Mark: sounds good. i'd also like to validate the on-prem topology assumptions — we've seen spikes during peak ingest and need to know if it was network or runtime.

[00:26] Priya: great. i'll start by restating what we're seeing — feel free to correct me. your telemetry shows steady p95 ~140-180ms but intermittent p99 spikes up to 720ms, mostly at higher concurrencies and correlated with certain prompt prefixes, correct?

[00:41] Lina: yes exactly, it's weird — some prefixes blow up the tail even at moderate QPS. we suspected KV cache misses but i don't think it's the whole story.

[00:52] Priya: okay. two quick axes: (1) server-side execution variance (kernel selection/quantization slow paths, memory stalls), (2) network hops and VPC on-prem egress jitter and (3) KV cache hotkeys. usually it's a combination.

[01:10] Samira: i'll add that batch dynamics matter — if batching window expands because of input distribution, you can see p95 stay okay but p99 jump when one request waits longer to fill a batch.

[01:24] Jamie: i want to focus on the network piece — our on-prem racks are dual-AZ within the colo and we've measured intra-az latency sub-ms but cross-az links sometimes get 8-30ms jitter. do you think that explains 700ms spikes? seems high.

[01:38] Priya: cross-AZ alone rarely produces 700ms unless it's compounded with a blocking op. example: a rare kernel fallback path for int8 dequantization could add 200-300ms, then a cross-AZ hop adds 20-30ms, plus queuing and a KV miss that cascades to a cold lookup — those add up. also if the request got retried or fell back to a slower model variant you can hit big tails.

[01:58] Mark: can you elaborate on kernel fallback? what causes that?

[02:03] Priya: sure — when we push quantized models (int8 / q4 variants) the runtime picks optimized kernels for most ops, but certain attention patterns or long position embeddings can trigger a different path, sometimes using a slower elementwise kernel or even an fp16 kernel if a fused int8 kernel isn't available. it's rare but expensive. sometimes it's input-length dependent, sometimes due to a specific op like RoPE handling.

[02:30] Lana (transcription mislabel): uh lina yeah.

[02:33] Lina: right, our product uses a lot of long-context prompts and a handful of system prefixes that are very common (hot keys). when the KV cache misses on those prefixes, the runtime has to recompute or fetch from cold storage — which is painful. we've seen correlation between hot prefixes and the highest p99s.

[02:52] Priya: that's the classic hotkey hotspot. two mitigations we recommend: (a) shard the KV cache by prefix hash to spread load across nodes, and (b) use a small local in-memory prefix cache on the serving instance for the top N prefixes. sharding prevents single-node saturation which creates large queuing delays.

[03:14] Omar: quick question — sharding sounds great but increases cross-node fetches. won't that add network hops?

[03:20] Samira: yes if you shard without co-location. the trick is co-locating shards or using consistent hashing so the serving runtime routes to the locally attached shard when possible. if co-location can't be guaranteed in your colo, we favor small in-instance LRU for top prefixes + asynchronous warmers for expected prefixes.

[03:38] Ethan: can i share a quick picture of how these pieces add? baseline latency = compute token time + KV lookup (if miss) + network egress time. tail arises when one component balloons (e.g., kernel fallback or KV node saturation) while others remain stable.

[03:57] Mark: the dashboard also shows occasional CPU steal on the hosts, could that be a factor?

[04:02] Priya: absolutely. CPU steals and noisy neighbors on shared infra can push long-tail if the runtime needs CPU for dequantize / CPU fallback ops. for on-prem, pinned cgroups or dedicated capacity helps a lot. that's actually one of the Redwood Dedicated selling points vs multi-tenant hosted.

[04:20] Nina: any tradeoffs we should be aware of if we move to streaming responses? our UX wants faster first-token and progressive tokens, but we are worried about consistency.

[04:30] Priya: streaming reduces perceived latency for user-facing first token and can lower some tail metrics because work is pipelined — but it increases connection time and ties up resources longer per request. streaming also complicates batching since you want to emit tokens while still maximizing throughput. for p99 it's nuanced: streaming can reduce p99 for long outputs (because you surface early tokens) but if network disconnects or retries occur, it can amplify tail because the session stays open.

[04:59] Lina: our typical responses are 80-400 tokens with heavy variance; user experience favors first-token fast and then steady stream. we did see improved p95 but inconsistent p99 after enabling streaming in our internal tests.

[05:14] Priya: that matches expectations. if you need steady tail controls, we recommend hybrid: streaming for small outputs + non-streamed for long-form, or streaming with short-lived batching windows and a max wait. also consider early-exit models for interactive queries.

[05:30] Samira: another lever is prefix caching — if your top prefixes are cached locally, the runtime can skip KV fetch and emit first token much faster, which helps both p95 and p99.

[05:40] Jamie: i want to make sure we understand the quantization impact. we had folks advocate q4 and int8 to save cost but worried about worst-case performance. what's your experience?

[05:49] Priya: quantization reduces memory bandwidth and improves throughput but can introduce slower code paths for certain ops as i mentioned. int8 often has excellent average performance, but q4 variants that use special packing may rely on custom kernels — if those kernels aren't available for a particular attention layout, we fall back. So test with your canonical prompts. also note hallucination risk isn't the only concern; decoding variance and timeouts are as important.

[06:12] Mark: ok — so action item: we'll produce a small canon prompt set that represents the hot prefixes and the long-form.

[06:18] Ethan: perfect, that'll help us recreate the tail. we'll run a stress bench with concurrency ramps and hotkey shuffles. we'll also enable instrumentation to log when the runtime chooses fallback kernels.

[06:29] Nina: about network: if we keep everything in one AZ, we lose redundancy, but cross-AZ increases jitter. any recommendations?

[06:36] Samira: typical pattern: keep latency-sensitive shards co-located for hot paths (same rack/az), and replicate asynchronously to other AZs for resilience. for border cases, use active-active with local routing and a fallback to remote if a local shard is saturated. that minimizes tail while preserving redundancy.

[06:55] Lina: how do we detect hotkey saturation in real time? our ops team needs alerts before p99 spikes hit users.

[07:02] Priya: instrument KV hit rates per-prefix, queue length per shard, and kernel fallback counters. set anomaly thresholds on per-prefix queue growth and long tail of time-to-first-byte. we'll share a dashboard template.

[07:16] Mark: are there any quick wins we can do before the bench? maybe change batching window or tune autoscaling?

[07:22] Priya: yes. short-term: reduce the max batching window to lower p99 at some throughput cost, enable prefix-level prewarming for the top 50 prefixes, and pin GPU/CPU resources for critical nodes. medium-term: implement sharded KV and calibrate quantized kernels with your prompt set.

[07:40] Jamie: curious about failover — if a KV shard is overloaded, can Redwood fallback to a smaller model locally to preserve latency?

[07:46] Priya: yes, runtime supports graceful degradation: route to a lightweight model variant or local cached completions for certain prefixes. you configure per-route fallback policies — we've seen this reduce error rates and tails in production.

[07:59] Ethan: quick note on measurement: please export p50/p95/p99 along with token distribution and concurrency levels — that helps us correlate. also include kernel-fallback logs and any tcp retransmit counts from your network team.

[08:12] Omar: we'll pull netstat/traceroute captures around the windows we saw spikes.

[08:18] Priya: good. one more gotcha — TLS termination and KMS calls can add non-trivial latency if KMS is synchronous on the critical path. ensure crypto ops are on the hot path only when necessary and consider caching decrypted keys in secure enclaves to avoid round trips.

[08:35] Mark: oh yeah, we saw a correlation between key-access peaks and some of the spikes. we assumed it was unrelated.

[08:42] Priya: it's related — KMS stalls are often correlated with billing or audit workloads that hit the same HSM cluster. separate those or cache tokens.

[08:52] Samira: ok let's summarize and close with concrete next steps.

[08:56] Ethan: summary recap: (1) Cygnus will provide prompt set and network diagram, (2) Redwood SEs to run bench and share perf spreadsheet + kernel-fallback counters, (3) short-term mitigations: tighten batching window, prefix prewarm, and pin resources, (4) medium-term: sharded KV + co-location and fallback model policies, (5) share security and on-prem packaging docs.

[09:27] Nina: that'll work. can we get an estimated timeline for the bench results?

[09:31] Priya: baseline bench in ~7 business days after we get prompts & topo, then an extended hotkey stress test a few days after. we'll put dates in CRM.

[09:40] Ethan: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the perf link and calendar invites.

[09:45] Mark: thanks all, appreciate the level of detail.

[09:48] Meeting ended.

Notes: transcript contains some speaker mislabels and typical ASR errors (e.g., "Vertext" vs "Vertex"). Links referenced during call: Perf spreadsheet: https://redwood.internal/perf/cygnus-bench-0928  , Security whitepaper & KMS checklist: https://redwood.docs/security/kms-onprem
